subtopic: PROVISION FOR INDICATION OF LIFE EXPECTANCY OF PRODUCT
PROVISION FOR INDICATION OF LIFE EXPECTANCY OF PRODUCT
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-203, to amend the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs Act.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INDICATION OF LIFE EXPECTANCY OF PRODUCT
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INDICATION OF LIFE EXPECTANCY OF PRODUCT
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to amend the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs Act to provide, so far as parliament may do so, that manufacturers
and marketers be required to indicate the life expectancy of their products. Many manufacturers now have a good idea how long a toaster or a light bulb will last, for example. If this bill is approved the consumer will also have that knowledge.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: SUMMERSIDE-REQUEST FOR DEFINITION OF STRATEGIC FUNCTION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SUMMERSIDE-REQUEST FOR DEFINITION OF STRATEGIC FUNCTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Minister of National Defence. Has he received a resolution passed by the legislature of Prince Edward Island urging the federal government to define and establish a strategic military function for the Canadian forces base at Summerside, assuring its continuation at present or increased levels of usefulness and activity?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUMMERSIDE-REQUEST FOR DEFINITION OF STRATEGIC FUNCTION
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member knows it is not sufficient simply to ask whether a telegram or resolution has been received.

subtopic: SUMMERSIDE-REQUEST FOR DEFINITION OF STRATEGIC FUNCTION
speechtext: Then may I rephrase my question and ask the minister if he would take this resolution under advisement in the hope that he might be able to give a reassuring statement to the house and to the people of Prince Edward Island in the near future.

speakeroldname: Hon. Leo Cadieux (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: SUMMERSIDE-REQUEST FOR DEFINITION OF STRATEGIC FUNCTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think I can give that reassuring statement right now. On Monday 1 had the privilege of meeting with the premier and a delegation from the province who came to present a brief on the use of the Summer-side base. I have declared, and I repeat, that the base is not going to be closed, that we are trying to maintain the highest possible level of military activity there, that we have received suggestions from the province which we are studying, and that we are going to meet in a couple of weeks' time to decide whether we can implement them.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REDUCTION IN STRENGTH OF ARMED FORCES

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REDUCTION IN STRENGTH OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of National Defence. speakeroldname: Hon. Leo Cadieux (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO REDUCTION IN STRENGTH OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
The way I understand it, Mr. Speaker, that is a speculative story. We have fixed the floor at 100,000 and I hope we can stay there. This is what I consider a minimum to meet the commitments that we have.

maintopic: MONTREAL-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO CONTROL PILFERAGE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: MONTREAL-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO CONTROL PILFERAGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Transport. In view of the serious dangers to the port of Montreal this coming shipping season-I believe the minister knows what those risks are-would he take into consideration the recommendations of the last eight inquiries into this situation and bring about some action before the shipping season opens in earnest next month?

maintopic: MONTREAL-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO CONTROL PILFERAGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, some action has already been taken. As my hon. friend might expect, the National Harbours Board has already acted in one of the most critical areas relating to pilferage. They have hired some of the most competent people available in the business to establish a police system to bring this abuse under control. They have confidence that the plans they have embarked on can cope, hopefully quite adequately, with what has been a very serious problem. Although an additional inquiry is being made I am sure that wherever action is possible, based on previous inquiries, it will not be held up just because another inquiry is under way.

maintopic: MONTREAL-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO CONTROL PILFERAGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Labour. Has the minister heard of any indications of an intention to hold lock-outs at the grain terminal plants in the port of Montreal this year?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: MONTREAL-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO CONTROL PILFERAGE
speechtext: have heard some rumours but I have no definite information.

maintopic: MONTREAL-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO CONTROL PILFERAGE
speechtext: You will wait for the crisis to develop. This is government by crisis.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION POLICIES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Transport. In view of mounting criticism from many ports in Canada, including Montreal, is the government considering a major reorganization of finance and administration policies with respect to these ports, and if so when will it be implemented?

March 1, 1968
Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION POLICIES
speechtext: This is a very major policy question, Mr. Speaker, but a study is being done to review the present operations of all ports, the different administrations which apply to them, and the relative success of the different forms of administration. Once this study has been done we will be in a better position to know what changes, if any, should be recommended so far as port administration is concerned.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION POLICIES
speechtext: As a supplementary question, can the minister say whether the government has in mind a method by which there would be a greater degree of local autonomy given to the ports?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION POLICIES
speechtext: Inevitably, Mr. Speaker, this is one of the questions which will be raised and hopefully answered, or at least dealt with in the inquiry. It is one of the things we would have to know before considering any alternative form of administration, whether it should be the same across the country or whether we need to have different forms to meet local conditions in different parts of the country.

subtopic: MANITOBA-THREATENED STRIKE AT FLIN FLON MINE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MANITOBA-THREATENED STRIKE AT FLIN FLON MINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Labour. Is the minister in a position to report on the threatened strike of the employees of Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company of Flin Flon, Manitoba, which was set for today?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: MANITOBA-THREATENED STRIKE AT FLIN FLON MINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his question. I might say that the strike deadline constituted a serious threat to the economy of Flin Flon. When I learned of it I dispatched a special mediator to the area about a week ago. I am happy to say I have just received a report that a tentative settlement was agreed upon yesterday and approved by a vote of the union members taken last night. It would seem that the threatened strike has been averted.

subtopic: JOHN STEPHEN MARSHALL-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF SENTENCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
subtopic: JOHN STEPHEN MARSHALL-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF SENTENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for

the minister of Indian affairs. Has he received any representations on behalf of John Stephen Marshall of the Eskasoni Indian reservation? I understand these representations were made by St. Francis Xavier University and the John Howard Society with regard to the charge of arson and subsequent severe sentence.
In view of the sad and regrettable circumstances surrounding the case would the minister please check with the Solicitor General and the Minister of Justice to see whether a reassessment could be made of this case?

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: JOHN STEPHEN MARSHALL-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF SENTENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am quite certain the hon. member would not wish me to comment on the quality of justice dispensed by Canadian courts. Recourse is available, and I understand an appeal is being organized on behalf of the man. Some of my officials think there are some extenuating circumstances, in that a new house was being constructed for the man and there was some evidence that he was in a hurry to get into it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Brelon North and Victoria):
subtopic: JOHN STEPHEN MARSHALL-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF SENTENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to pose a supplementary question with regard to John Stephen Marshall. In view of the fact that the minister did not indicate in his reply that he will institute an inquiry, may I direct my question to the Solicitor General. Is he aware that this man has suffered long term unemployment, which is rampant in his region; that he suffered from alcoholism, which is rampant across Canada; that he could not speak English, only Mic-Mac; and was not represented by defence counsel? Could he, in view of these extenuating circumstances, cause an inquiry to be held?

subtopic: JOHN STEPHEN MARSHALL-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF SENTENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot add anything to the answer given by my colleague the Minister for Indian Affairs and Northern Development, but I will discuss the matter with him.

maintopic: ROUTE TO BE FOLLOWED BY EXPORTS TO JAPAN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: ROUTE TO BE FOLLOWED BY EXPORTS TO JAPAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. I apologize for not having given him notice, but there is a good deal of
March 1, 1968

interest in the west with regard to the shipping of Fernie coal to the coast. Has the minister anything further to report to the house with regard to the shipment of this coal to Canadian Pacific ports?

maintopic: ROUTE TO BE FOLLOWED BY EXPORTS TO JAPAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is not very much I can add to what has been said already. Negotiations with the company are continuing, and I am still hopeful that the coal will be carried by Canadian carriers to the lower mainland port. I still believe this is essential so far as Canadian interests are concerned, and we are assuming that this will be the case.

subtopic: QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF ABITIBI AS DESIGNATED AREA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF ABITIBI AS DESIGNATED AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the hon. Minister of Industry.
In view of the fact that some industries would readily settle in Abitibi, an area which has been neglected for many years, does the hon. minister intend to include that area in the list of designated areas?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF ABITIBI AS DESIGNATED AREA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the selection of designated areas is made after studying the unemployment statistics. There is no question of discretion or selection other than that based on the study of unemployment statistics.

subtopic: QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF ABITIBI AS DESIGNATED AREA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask a supplementary question. Is the minister aware of the fact that several hundred people in Abitibi, particularly in La Sarre area, are forced to go and find work in the neighbouring province of Ontario? Is he also aware of the fact that this latter region is considered to be a designated area and that the industries which are now thinking of locating at La Sarre would consider going to Ontario, if Abitibi is not recognized as a designated area?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF ABITIBI AS DESIGNATED AREA
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF ABITIBI AS DESIGNATED AREA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, has the minister received representations by the organized bodies of the northwestern Quebec area asking him to include the area in the list of designated areas?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF ABITIBI AS DESIGNATED AREA
speechtext:
Not personally, Mr. Speaker, but I shall inquire into it, in order to find out if representations have been made to the department.
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT OF DAIRY COMMISSION LEGISLATION

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO OPPORTUNITY FOR HOUSE DISCUSSION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO OPPORTUNITY FOR HOUSE DISCUSSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Acting Prime Minister whether, in planning the work of this house for the remainder of this session, any consideration is being given to setting aside a day or two to discuss the constitutional questions the Prime Minister had in mind before the defeat of the government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO OPPORTUNITY FOR HOUSE DISCUSSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the first thing I should like to say to the hon. gentleman is that I am sure all of us in this house are very glad to see him in his seat today after a long interval of serious illness.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO OPPORTUNITY FOR HOUSE DISCUSSION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO OPPORTUNITY FOR HOUSE DISCUSSION
speechtext: The Prime Minister indicated, I think on Wednesday, that the government would have been happy to consider in this house last week the constitutional conference and its implications. We regard this as a very important matter, and we will have to consider this further manifestation of interest in this vital problem that faces the Canadian people at this time.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO OPPORTUNITY FOR HOUSE DISCUSSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would you request the Acting Prime Minister to give us several days advance notice of any plan to hold such a debate?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO OPPORTUNITY FOR HOUSE DISCUSSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will be acquainted with the program which faces parliament in its ensuing days.

March 1. 1968

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO IMPROVED SECURITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Transport whether he is taking urgent steps to improve security at large Canadian airports, in view of the robbery that is reported to have taken place at the Montreal airport last night.

speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Has the minister any reason to suspect that this robbery was carried out by a paramilitary organization?

speechtext: Yes, I think it was.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had a question for the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who was floating around the chamber a few moments ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. House again in committee of supply, supplementary estimates (C), 1967-68, of the Department of Agriculture. Shall vote 5c carry?
Mr. Chairman, may I inquire whether the minister wishes to make a statement at this time?

Mr. Chairman, since we are discussing supplementary estimates rather than main estimates, at the end of our deliberations I will attempt to answer any questions hon. members may have, if this meets with the approval of the committee.

Mr. Chairman, for weeks the members of this party, many of whom either are now or in previous years have been actively engaged in the industry of agriculture in order to make a living, have been waiting impatiently for these supplementary estimates of the Department of Agriculture to be brought into this parliament. It is my personal opinion that no pestilence, plant disease, drought, flood or any other act of God has done more collective damage to agriculture on a national basis than this Liberal government. This statement would normally be considered one of partisan politics, but by documentation I shall show that unfortunately for this industry it is simply a statement of fact.

March 1, 1968
Supply-A griculture
This government and its spokesmen both inside and outside parliament have constantly assured Canadian farmers that all was well; that the gross national product of farms was rising; that efficiency of production was still increasing; that prices of farm products under their administration were constantly rising; in short, Mr. Chairman, that farmers had never had it so good. I know from experience that they can no doubt produce the necessary figures to support this fairy tale, but I should like in the next few moments to indicate to this committee the almost hopeless economic quagmire that the action or lack of action of these hon. members opposite has created for the farmers of Canada who are trying to earn a living.
It is my intention, Mr. Chairman, to deal with the subject in broad and general terms only, for I shall be followed by colleagues in my party who shall be most specific and detailed; and, commodity by commodity, we hope to place before the members of this house the grim realities of the economic chaos facing nearly every agricultural endeavour in Canada today. The government says the farmers have never had it so good. I wonder whether the government is absolutely blind to conditions as they exist in this country today. Never had it so good, Mr. Chairman? Within the last 12 months we have had the largest protest march in the history of Canada right here on parliament hill by thousands of angry farmers protesting the policy or lack of policy of this government.
Never had it so good, Mr. Chairman? We have witnessed tractor demonstrations, protest meetings, farmers on picket lines, threats of food boycotts, violence, petitions to governments, closing of cheese factories, food canneries, food processing plants, a sugar refinery and creameries on a scale never dreamed possible in this country. We have seen segments of the industry, such as early fruits and vegetables, wool production and the greenhouse industry driven to such low economic levels that in large areas of Canada they are being abandoned entirely.
Never had it so good, Mr. Chairman? Let me give you a few examples of headlines that have appeared in farm papers, market reports and newspapers across the country. These are a few gathered at random. The first one appeared in the Blenheim News Tribune for February 15: "Winter wheat export worst in ten years". That does not refer to western wheat, Mr. Chairman, but to the soft winter wheat produced in eastern Canada.

Another headline in the same publication reads "Artificial products threat to dairy industry". This headline is from the Kent Farmer for November 20: "Farm subsidies not the answer". Another one reads "Soya bean growers ask investigation". From the Western Producer, February 22, 1967, under the heading "Promoting and protecting wheat sales" there is the comment "Canadian wheat export sales drastically reduced". Another headline in the same publication reads "Export drop hits soya bean industry". Then from the Windsor Star for February 10: "Quota fight threatens dairy farmers". Another headline reads "Times are real rough down on the farm". Then this headline appeared in the Farm and Country, published in Toronto, January 23: "Death threatens Ontario greenhouse industry". Another headline from the same publication for February 27 reads "Ontario Federation of Agriculture suggests plant seizure". This was a reference to the unfortunate closure of the sugar refinery at Chatham, bringing with it hardship to all the local sugar beet growers. Then from The Grower for October, 1967: "Brief asks for action on Australian imports". Again The Grower for February, 1968: "Does the strawberry industry have a future in Ontario?". That publication also carried this headline: "Kingsville plant closed". This had reference to the food processing plant of Canadian Canners Limited, which for years had canned peaches, potatoes and tomatoes.
You can hardly pick up a trade paper today, Mr. Chairman, without being faced with similar headlines, such as "Grade A price of eggs to producer sags to 200". The same type of headline is found with regard to nearly every section of agriculture. One headline reads, "Grade A Price Of Eggs To Producer Sags To 200 Per Day". Another reads, "Hog Prices Continue To Decline". Still another reads, "Beef Prices Down J0 Pound". And so it goes on.
[DOT] (12 noon)
Never had it so good? Economic forecasts for agriculture predict that gross income for farmers in 1968 will equal that of 1967 but rising costs will cut millions from net returns in 1968.
Never had it so good? The farmers of this nation are $800 million deeper in debt today than they were just ten years ago.
March 1, 1968

Never had it so good? Ernie Bezaire, a veteran farm reporter for the Windsor Star, on Saturday, February 10 put it this way:
Farmers in southwestern Ontario would have to go back to the bitter 30's to find more troublesome times than they are now experiencing in agriculture.
In all fairness it must be said that world conditions and trade patterns directly affect our own industry. Other governments, however, immediately put into effect countermeasures to protect their own agricultural industries. But our government procrastinates, waffles, blunders and finally dashes into ill conceived action which has brought us almost to the point of economic annihilation.
The government may have meant well in its agricultural policy but may I, by citing some prime examples, show clearly that the government was either ill informed, ill advised, or just did not care. I shall deal first with administration. The government contended that in this modern day and age efficiency and decision were only possible by centralized departments and a chain of command. Hence it staked its political life on this policy and amalgamated the armed forces into a unified service. What about agriculture? In personnel the department is almost as big as the armed services. In this time of crisis in the agricultural industry the government went counter to its policy. It split responsibility for agriculture among the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
What has been the result of this action? The result is that we have the greatest possible confusion in this sector.
Second, the Minister of Agriculture races pell-mell on a course of action deliberately designed, as he has announced time and again, to move the small farmers of Canada-I believe he estimates them to be about 30 per cent of all farmers-off the land in order to make farms into sound, viable economic units and to create stability in agriculture. This is a popular argument but this policy collapses immediately when government action or inaction removes the profitable market for these so-called economic units. That is what happened when it allowed the deluge of imported canned fruits, meats, turkeys and, yes, eggs. Now we have the bankruptcy of the largest of these so-called stabilized farm units and have witnessed the recent
Supply-Agriculture
bankruptcies of three large greenhouse firms in a single week. The government should learn. In the United States over 50,000 of these large economic units have collapsed in the last few years.
Third, the governmen says, "Move the farmers off the farms and retrain them." But what does the government do? It starts this program and then cuts off grants to build and finance technical schools where such training should take place. Consequently farm families are left to migrate to the nearest urban centre and to compete as unskilled labour for second class jobs.
Fourth, the government has constantly encouraged commodity groups in agriculture to police their own industries. They are told, "Cut down production; tailor your production to meet the domestic market." That sounds good and reads well. Farmers have complied faithfully only to find that the limited domestic market has been swamped with cheap imports when they have been ready to supply it.
Fifth, by advocating efficiency of production and larger economic units and by making credit easy the government has encouraged Canadian farmers to borrow millions of dollars to enlarge their businesses and improve their efficiency. Now the government has the effrontery to say that under the Kennedy tariff round some farmers will have to go, that there may be a temporary period when they will have to be phased out and go into some other agricultural endeavour. Any government that thinks like this knows absolutely nothing about modern agriculture.
Hear, hear.

The capital investment
required and the vast technical knowledge and special equipment needed in farming make it virtually impossible these days for farmers to change their fields of endeavour. If they did, in most instances the result would be economic ruin. Some farmers who financed their farms knew that it would take at least a generation to pay off the debt. That was done deliberately. Therefore, to speak of phasing out now is absolute nonsense.
Sixth, I wish to speak of long-range plans. To create economic units, as the government has suggested should be done, requires a tremendous amount of capital, absolute business management and indispensable long-range planning. By its bungling the government has caused tremendous damage. Its long-range policies do well to last the test of one year.

March 1, 1968
Supply-Agriculture
As prime examples of my contention I cite the three different dairy policies we have had in three years and the government's on again, off again, turkey import quotas.
Seventh, the confusion in the dairy industry would be comic if it were not so tragic. Dairy farmers in Ontario today are placed in an untenable position. Federal policy is explicitly directed toward shutting down small producers and forcing large units to produce greater volumes more efficiently. At the same time a provincial policy places limited quotas on producers, thus making expansion into larger production units almost impossible. Who says farmers never had it so good? Through the Department of Agriculture the government spends the taxpayers' money to expand tobacco production; through the Department of National Health and Welfare it spends the taxpayers' money to curtail the domestic consumption of tobacco.
Never had it so good? Our young people and our old people are leaving the land by the thousands. Our best cattle are being dispersed all over the world. Our best farm land is being covered with concrete and buildings. Our domestic markets are fast shrinking under the constant pressure of cheap imports. Canadian agriculture, once great and world admired, has been reduced to a state of clawing frantically for survival.
The government constantly whines when it is confronted with these facts. It asks, "What did you do when you were in power? Where were your policies?" When we were in office our policy was designed to keep farmers on the farms if they wanted to stay.
Hear, hear.

We deliberately encouraged young people to choose farming as a way of life. Certainly we made mistakes, but much of our policy remains as a background to this government's policies. And our policy was tailored to meet the challenges of 1956, not of 1968.
As to our policy now, our leader will take part in this debate and he will put our ideas before the house. I must emphasize, however, that we believe there are three categories of farmers today and that all are absolutely essential to Canada. We have the part-time farmer, the family farmer and the corporate farmer, and no blanket policy can possibly meet all their needs.
Never had it so good? God help the Canadian farmer in this hour of his agony.
[Mr. Danforth.l
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)

I am pleased to see the hon.
member for Kootenay East assisting the Minister of Agriculture today. This may be evidence of new thought within the government, particularly since Cominco has been interested in agriculture for some time-I am thinking of the fertilizer industry-and I am sure that in the days ahead the minister may have some use for the advice which Cominco can provide.
This is not the occasion for a major debate on agriculture and we do not intend to treat it as such. But these supplementary estimates, the tag ends of the main estimates, do ask for a further $33 million for the Department of Agriculture. As I see it, the major problems facing the industry are those which have been mentioned by the hon. member for Kent (Ont.), and some of them arise out of government legislation whose implications have still to be faced.
For a long time there has been a general desire that agriculture should become more efficient. Farmers have agreed with this concept and have improved their operations with the result that there is far greater efficiency today in the dairy industry, for example, than there was in the past. This is true with regard to many other crops and farming activities. Yet we are still troubled by the difficulties facing farmers who live on marginal land, cultivating it as agricultural holdings when it should probably be used for some other purpose under the ARDA program. This program was supported by most members of parliament; yet great anomalies are arising from its operation. Dairy farmers have encountered many difficulties. A market for milk at $5 f.o.b. factory has resulted in an improvement in the incomes of farmers engaged in milk production, but the government's action a year ago in discontinuing payments on secondary milk has had an adverse effect on many producers whose net incomes have been sharply reduced. The government will have to do something about this situation.
It is true that production of milk should, if it is to be economic, bear a close relation to consumption. But if in the past the price support system we used resulted in a surplus, the type of program now being followed is likely to result in a limited number of farmers receiving a much larger share of revenue from production. Using large blocks of land and capital they will be operating on a scale much bigger than any which normal farmers could expect to reach. Eventually this may
March 1, 1968

give rise to a situation in which Canadian consumers find themselves paying a great deal more for milk products because of their relative scarcity. This prospect has to be taken into consideration by the government when it is considering other aspects of policy with regard to the dairy industry.
Farmers will disagree, but it is my opinion that when a shortage of butter developed during the war the farm organizations should have asked the federal government to go into the production of margarine. Had this been done the farmers would have been able to control the relationship between margarine and butter. But they did not. In the event, the public outcry was so great that production and sale of margarine were allowed by law and since that time the product has been in direct competition with butter.
The market for margarine is a lucrative one. Those responsible for its production and marketing have been able to regulate the selling price with an eye to butter prices and have been able to parley the relatively small cost of production to a point where the return to the industry is a highly profitable one. In some cases, shrewd advertising has enabled the prices of oil substitutes to be raised until they are at a premium.
New products are being developed in agriculture, and their appearance should cause concern both to the department and to the farm organizations. It is surprising the number of things that can be done with our natural products. I am sure those who normally eat butter would find it difficult to be altogether certain today whether they were eating fresh butter or a substitute. Similarly, where there is a choice between fluid milk or reconstituted milk, or what is called multimilk, a condensed product, users would find it difficult to be sure which had been reconstituted and which had come from the farm in fluid form.

We know that this milk was reconstituted by using skim milk and other additives and that it was a very palatable product. Since that time we have become much more sophisticated in developing substitutes for milk. Now we have 27053-452

The Department of Agriculture should be concerned about these developments. It should take steps in conjunction with farm organizations not to stop these developments but to discover how they can be integrated with the present agricultural program. These developments will continue whether we like them or not. What we are interested in is that they cause the least dislocation possible.
When the minister is preparing his estimates for next year he should provide funds for legislation to make it easier for young people to establish themselves on economic agricultural units. A few years ago a young person had to find $25,000 to start farming. Now the amount required is probably double.
At the opening of the Saskatchewan dam, as I am interested in irrigation I was concerned to see the type of farmers who attended the ceremony. I think most of them present would have holes in their heads if they were to become interested in irrigation. They were the original pioneer farmers, ranging in age from 50 to 70, and at that age it is unthinkable that they would buy the necessary equipment to instal irrigation facilities. The generation following them will have to do that, but a great deal of capital will be required.
If young people are to be encouraged to enter farming the government will have to make some changes in succession duties on land. The one thing which has risen even faster than the cost of living is the price of land. It is safe to say that if a man bought a mountain top ten years ago he could get twice as much today as he paid for it, no matter whether it has a useful purpose or not.
The rise in the price of land has been caused to some extent by farms on the outskirts of cities being bought for subdivisions. They are bought for prices ranging from $400,000 to $500,000 and the result is that other farmers believe their farms have an equivalent value. This may be all very well if they can sell their land but if they die before doing so the valuation made of their property is so great that estate duties demand that their families liquidate their holdings. Often the money left over after paying succession duties is insufficient to establish a surviving son in farming.

allow us to enter world markets not only in respect of wheat, butter and cheese but in respect of a number of other agricultural products. With the technology available to farmers today and the assistance we hope can be provided to them I am sure we will have a viable agricultural economy which will be able to hold its own and meet competition in world markets. This can be done only if the agricultural department moves forward quickly to meet the challenge facing the new generation which is entering the farming field today under totally new conditions.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few words to say about those supplementary estimates since they are related to a matter which is quite important in my area, namely agriculture.
I would have liked the minister to give us an outline of his future agricultural policy, because it is always interesting for a member of this house and for the farmers of an area to know a few months in advance what can be expected from the authorities.
I know that the duty of the federal Minister of Agriculture is, in the first place, to inquire about every possible production throughout Canada and to provide markets. In order to reach that objective effectively, the department must discover new markets, and then protect and encourage them.
As concerns finding international markets which are of interest to Canada in general, I think that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) should get assistance from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) whose duty it is precisely to contact and visit other countries in order to assess trade possibilities.
I understand that the minister's duties are not very easy at this time. I have been a member of the committee on agriculture, forestry and rural development for six years and I had the opportunity to go and see for myself agricultural developments in other provinces. In fact, it is only since then that I really understand the minister's duties and all the difficluties he could come up against to guarantee markets to farmers because, in the final analysis, that is where success lies for the farmer. If we want production to be stable and profitable enough so that farmers can make a living, it is imperative to have a market that can absorb not only a part of production but the whole production. That is why I said earlier that the minister should insist on greater assistance from the Minister 27053-452J

of Trade and Commerce in his exacting work of finding markets.
I also said that the government had to protect those international markets. Well and good to enter into agreements; but they must be beneficial to Canada and to Canadian producers. As a matter of fact, I had the opportunity yesterday, when our party met with the representatives of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, to refer to the dairy industry and the egg market. But should only those two questions be dealt with?
We are told that United States sales of dairy products have reached about the same level as ours. In my opinion, in looking into the dairy problem, the minister should be able, with the help of all his technicians, to further promote the development of that industry, since it is a major one, especially in the eastern provinces and in Ontario. We claim that an agreement which allows the United States to sell 50 per cent of the products in a given industry is not really advantageous for the Canadian farmers.
For instance, with regard to the production of eggs, we are allowed a proportion of 65 per cent. I feel that if the federal government could guarantee the markets, the province of Quebec and the eastern provinces could produce far more than they do now under the present agreements.
Mr. Chairman, I am mentioning those examples only to give you an idea of the advantages certain agreements could bring. We are told that they are meant to protect international markets, the market between the United States and Canada. I understand that, but on studying those agreements, one realizes that they are always a bit more favourable to the United States and less so for the small countries or Canada. Therefore, I am calling the hon. minister's attention to this matter.

We have, in the province of Quebec, a highly diversified agricultural production. We are not placed in the same situation as the western provinces which are mainly concerned with grain production and beef.

Mr. Chairman, as I said a moment ago, we had the good fortune of meeting with the representatives of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, who presented us with a most interesting report.
We would invite the Minister of Agriculture-besides, he must have met the very able federation advisers-to receive the advice of these experts, for I think that these men, who are chosen by the people each in his own area, that is to say by the C.F.U. members and those of other agricultural organizations, are much closer to the farmers and can act more decisively, precisely because they live in their midst. I would not say that they are more competent than the federal experts, but I think it would be advantageous for the latter to meet regularly with these people who have been delegated by various groups in each area to come to Ottawa and offer suggestions.

Canada should support the proposals the international dairy committee of the International Federation of Agricultural Producers submitted to GATT, which won solid support, for the creation of an international council of dairy products of which producers as well as governments would be members.
Mr. Chairman, I shall not dwell on that brief, but I should like to point out the quotas. I think that, in our region today, the greatest concern is centred on this question of quotas. As you know, work has been done in this connection in the past few years, but we in the Lake St. John region are going through a period of transition: from spare-time farmers, so to speak, we are becoming real farmers, for agriculture in our region was formerly a rather marginal occupation, because of the proximity of lumber enterprises. We were a large family of farmers, 50 per cent of whom worked the land while 50 per cent worked in the forest.
One day, we woke up to find that only 18 per cent of our manpower was needed in the forest. Therefore, 90 per cent of the sons of farmers must come back to their farms.

I think that transition is very difficult to make in our areas. I should like the hon. Minister o f Agriculture to be aware of that state of affairs, when he deals with our people, because when the herd is not big enough, the quantity of milk is not sufficient, and so on.

If the herds are to become economic, they must grow and multiply. These farmers must also be given the opportunity not to sell their herds but to increase them. I say this because, unfortunately, that was the advice given to farmers by some investigators. I have never met these investigators, or you may be sure I would have had a few words to say to them. Their advice to the farmer is: Your herd is too small; sell it and move to town.
I know that this is not the minister's idea, since he wants the small farmers to become more productive and even to produce at full capacity, which would allow them to live on their farm. I think we will have to proceed by stages, and not make a complete change in one year and then say: Those who produce less than 12,000 to 20,000 pounds of milk will no longer receive help. On the contrary, I feel that it is with farmers who produce 12,000, 20,000 and 40,000 pounds that we will eventually succeed in having farmers who produce 150,000, 200,000 and 300,000 pounds. I know a great many who are willing to go ahead, but they need a little help from the government.
I should like to deal briefly with the mechanization aspect, one of the greatest problems in my area. Too much mechanization is required to make the land more productive and the herd more profitable. There again, I feel the government should make an effort and take the advice of organizations so as to try and reduce the price of farm machinery. I have sold farm machinery myself for ten years, and I am astonished at the fantastically increased prices. This is ridiculous.
In my opinion, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce would be in the best position to inquire into that, so that farmers can get the machinery, not free of charge, but at a reasonable price, because that is now strictly necessary.
It is often said that farmers are extravagant in some ways, that they are completely mechanized and that they invest all their

money in machinery. What else can they do? We are no longer living in the horse and buggy age. We are in the age of mechanization. Formerly, a horse and carriage were a necessity for the farmers. Today, they need a motor car to go to town and do their shopping.
It is imperative that we help the farmer to adapt himself to modern times. The government must understand the farmer's predicament. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will carry on the good work he is doing.
Comparisons can be made when a man is doing his best. I would not want to be too critical. I believe the Minister of Agriculture is doing his best, but he is not able to do everything he wants. Therefore, I ask him to carry on his work and, above all, increase the amount of help given to these farmers, who ask nothing more than to lead a decent life on their farms.

Mr. Chairman, when I began my remarks earlier I referred to the agricultural industry as an industry under siege, encircled, beleaguered, bombarded by rising costs, by low prices and by foreign imports. The list of its difficulties is long. I am sure many branches of the industry see the Department of Agriculture and the policies of the government as being one more force with which to contend. I would not want to

the $5 million worth of raw sugar that Canada imported. The sugar industry is aware of this and has made repeated submissions to the government to do something to develop a national sugar policy which would allow the Canadian industry to survive. This policy will be needed sooner than we realize, Mr. Chairman.
In a recent speech the general manager of B.C. Tree Fruits Limited of the Okanagan valley dwelt on this topic. In the course of his remarks he said:
The government is continually asking industry to expand its export markets. Yet, at the same time, it does not seem to be interested in the fact that the Canadian industry is losing out to foreign government subsidized imports. If Canadian industry is going to compete for world markets, it must first be in a position to compete on the domestic market.
The present tariffs allow both the United States and Australia to undersell Canadian products. On June 12th, 1967, Australian peaches were being offered in Toronto for $7.62 per case compared to $8.63 for the Canadian and $8.31 for the American product. In addition, Australia was offering a 30 cent per case promotional allowance to the retailer. The Australian industry has established a policy whereby the price quoted in Canada is below any product on the market.
I am sure no one would challenge the proposition if this price differential came about solely as a result of the initiative, energy and vigour of the fruit industry in Australia. The speech continues:
The Australian industry's ability to sell at such low prices is due to Australian government policies. Export incentives are made up of payroll tax rebate, double income tax deduction (200 per cent) on all expenditures made on export promotion. Funds are also made available from an excise duty applied to the sale of domestic fruit in Australia. It is expected that $1,800,000 ($2,160,000 Can.) will be available from this excise duty for export promotion in 1967.
The cumulation of these tax benefits, rebates on tin plate and sugar gives Australian processors an advantage of $2 or more per case of fruit. This advantage is used to obtain shelf space in our Canadian supermarkets at the expense of Canada's domestic production.
It is very evident tht the Australian government works in very close co-operation with their fruit processing industry to develop programs of assistance. In comparison, the Canadian tender fruit industry feels that tariff protection has too often been sacrificed to obtain concessions for other Canadian products.
Then he points to some reasons why the processing industry is so important to the Canadian fruit industry. He says:
The fruit growing industry is dependent on the processing industry in two ways. During the last ten years the processing industry has purchased 43 per cent of the apricots, 45 per cent of the
Supply-Agriculture
peaches and 47 per cent of the pears produced in Canada. If the fruit growers lost this market for their product the impact on the fresh fruit market would be disastrous.
Then the following recommendations are made to the government:
1.	Immediately opening negotiations with the Australian government to renegotiate the 1960 Australian trade agreement act to rescind the concessions accorded tender fruit imports.
2.	Reviewing the Australian tax incentives applicable to their tender fruit industry. If considered a direct subsidy, appropriate action should be taken to reinstate our Canadian anti-dumping legislation with Australia. If not a direct subsidy, Canadian legislation should be implemented to remove inequities.
3.	Establishing import tariffs equal to those enjoyed by Canadian competitors.
4.	Establishing a quota system as a temporary measure.
5.	If it is not possible to remove the present inequities, the Canadian government was asked to establish a subsidy program similar to that offered sugar beet, poultry, dairy and other industries.
6.	In co-operation with the industry, establishing a promotional program for the domestic and international markets.
7.	In co-operation with the growers and processors, conducting an economic survey of the tender fruit growing and processing industry, with the objective of determining ways of making the industry more competitive.
These are some of the measures that can be taken and some of the problems that can be investigated so far as one aspect of Canadian agriculture is concerned which is important not just to my constituency but to several sections of the country. This is not the first time that these matters have been raised. The industry has raised them repeatedly for several years and is beginning to despair of any effective action being initiated by this government.
The dairy industry is also under attack. It too is moving to meet the opposition that confronts it. It is moving very rapidly to modernize the industry, as is the fruit industry. It will not do to say that Canadian production is inefficient or that it is low in quality because this is not the case. Quality in the fruit industry, particularly in the apple industry of British Columbia, is unmatched anywhere. The modernization of the entire industry also has no equal.
For example, this past year the highest price per box of apples ever obtained in history was achieved on the New York market, so this is an indication of the quality of the products of the industry and the vigour with which it has moved to meet its problems.

However, more needs to be done. A coordinated national approach to agriculture by the federal government is required and it has not yet been made.
The dairy industry is moving toward such an approach. The brief of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture dwelt on its problems as well as on the problems of the poultry farmers, the grain producers and a vast number of other sections of the Canadian agricultural industry. When the brief came to my desk I read it with great interest. First of all I looked to see what were the recommendations of the industry in regard to the substitute products that are moving into the milk products market. When I talked to representatives of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture the other day I expressed disappointment that they had treated this subject so tentatively. I say this because they have not much time, and neither has the federal government, to decide what will be their approach toward this new threat to the dairy industry.
I am sure hon. members saw a short program on television the other evening about an enterprising manufacturer who is busy turning out a substitute for milk to be sold in plastic cartons. He did not call it milk but it is to be sold as suitable for many purposes for which milk has traditionally been used. He admitted that his product did not have the food value or quality of milk, and I imagine that many people listening to the program and learning of the constituents of the product said to themselves, "What stuff!" However, the manufacturer went on to say that there would be a 5 per cent price differential per quart compared with real milk. I suspect that it suddenly became tasty to many who viewed the program. But do people realize the basic importance of Canadian agriculture to this country?
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
If the word gets around that there is a substitute for milk which will sell for about 5 cents a quart less, the minister will have a battle on his hands and it will not only be with the Minister of Trade and Commerce but also with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. He knows that he cannot expect sympathy from housewives who are fighting soaring prices and he will not get much assistance from the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, since it was designed to look after the welfare of consumers.

I thought it was a mistake to alter the name of the department to consumer and corporate affairs. It should have been left alone.
The Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs ought to investigate the relationships among the big international soap companies which operate in this country. The department should investigate how synthetics are being used to manufacture foods. These companies have the resources and raw materials to manufacture soap and they could easily diversify into the manufacture of synthetic and substitute foods. That is why the dairy industry hesitates; it is not sure what is happening and it wants to find means to counter this threat. Those means, I suspect, lie in the powers of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Department of Agriculture and in the trade policies of the government. We should stop using cheap labour, inadequate living conditions, starvation and the host of other problems that beset the undeveloped nations of the world to bring Canadian agriculture to its knees. It is time we came up with policies which will ensure that our commodities fetch a decent price in the markets of the world and that our industries compete on a fair basis with their competitors around the world.
In the time that remains to him as head of this department I trust the minister will take steps to set in motion studies aimed at developing this type of policy for Canadian agriculture. I trust that he and his officials will pay the closest attention to the brief that has been presented by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I commend to the minister paragraph 39. It suggests how the desperate problems facing Canadian agriculture can be overcome. The brief recommends a minimum income policy, something that is widely discussed today and has ramifications far beyond the agricultural field.
Yesterday a columnist in a Toronto newspaper described the Minister of Justice as the next Prime Minister of Canada, suggesting he was the William Aberhart of the present day. That is a startling statement, indeed, but we know that the government has finally had to consider policies that were put forward by social credit in 1935, having to do with distribution of income throughout the population. Though I do not particularly wish the Minister of Justice well, I hope, should he succeed in rising to the high office of prime minister, that he will live up to the billing he got yesterday in the Toronto papers.

The brief spoke of an early retirement policy for farmers and of retraining and re-establishment policies. These are absolutely vital to the dairy industry in view of the announcement of January 15 about the 196869 dairy subsidy quota policy. We know that the subsidy policy has been tightened considerably. This policy, which is approved by large sections of industry, is aimed at eliminating some of the small operators. The quotas are designed to assist the development of larger production units. I think this policy is wise, and the government must persist with it. At the same time it should realize that when it no longer gives a subsidy to one who has been subsidized but gives the money to another, something of value has been lost by a member of the community and he should receive some sort of compensation. I say this because the government has caused the Canadian dairy industry grave problems by the sudden shifts in dairy policy over the last couple of years.
It would be well for the government to consider, in conjunction with the Department of Forestry and Rural Development, whether an early retirement policy could be developed for farmers. Such a policy would not leave the farmer who is 60 out in the cold, with a devalued farm which he must sell in a hurry because he has no income. The government must establish retraining and re-establishment policies and policies of farm consolidation. It might well look into the question of capital grants for farm improvement. The government knows how successful direct grants have been to industries in designated areas.
It is time the government saw the agricultural industry as an industry that requires the same consideration and care as the general manufacturing or drug industries of Canada. The other day we moved delicately to take steps that may lower drug prices in Canada. The government would never stand for profits of several hundred per cent in the agricultural industry, though the drug industry has enjoyed such profits for generations.
The government can do much to ensure that our agricultural industry is competitive. Our agricultural industry is more valuable than the mere products it produces. It is valuable to this nation in ways different from any other industry. The tourist industry depends on the agricultural industry indirectly. If farms go to waste and lie fallow, if buildings collapse and become shabby, the beauty of the countryside is spoiled and the
Supply-Agriculture
beauty of our countryside, the beauty of rural Canada, is a great attraction to tourists.
Although he may not be able to clean up all of agriculture's problems immediately, I hope the minister can iron out some of the problems connected with the computer used in the distribution of dairy subsidy cheques. The department should ask whoever sold the computer to refund the money or provide a new model. On the other hand, if it is a question of personnel more should be hired to make the computer work properly, or perhaps we should train the people we have so they can operate the computer properly. I am tired of telling dairy producers in my constituency, as I am sure every member with dairy farmers in his constituency is, that the computer has broken down. I say, "It will be ready in another week. I know your creditors are at your door but the cheque will arrive next week." Next week, when nothing has happened, I have to send out a letter saying, "Sorry, but the computer konked out again. The cheque will come some time next month; it will arrive. All you have to do is hold on. Hold on and the cheque will get to you." I hope that in the near future we can be assured that the computer problems have been taken care of and that cheques will go out sufficiently regularly to raise the morale of those in one part of our dairy industry who badly need a boost.
