speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I was favourably impressed by the fact that my colleagues on this side of the house who took part in the agricultural debate made brief and direct speeches. I hope to follow their example in commenting on this bill, which I understand an hon. member may move to have referred to the standing committee, if it passes on second reading today.
In my view the control of pollution in Canada is one of the most urgent and serious matters we now face. It consists not only of

having clean air and clean water, because there is a more fundamental problem involved in it. Until pollution is under control, our industrial production cannot continue at an accelerating rate because as production increases, so does pollution. Not only must we reduce the pollution which exists at present, but we must control any pollution in the future. Production by large industries inevitably brings about pollution of air and water, sometimes at the same time and by the same factory. This must be controlled before new industry starts. So we cannot accelerate production until this problem is controlled, and regulations for new industry are introduced all across Canada.
Second, we cannot hope to attract an increasing number of visitors to Canada if our reputation for clean air and clean water is not maintained; and it is well known that we intend to maintain our reputation, so as to encourage the flow of visitors. Finally, our quality of life will suffer if pollution is not controlled; and, after all, quality of life is our ultimate objective.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
However, even if the bill were adopted, Mr. Speaker, I think it is far from being an outright assault on the problem of air pollution, which in itself is only one segment of the whole area of pollution. Some people feel you really cannot separate air pollution from soil or water pollution, from the administrative point of view. Many industries pollute air, soil and water simultaneously. However I would not want to niggle about division of responsibility, because the main problem in Canada now in connection with pollution control is division of responsibility. There are so many commissions, organizations and levels of government involved that from the action point of view we have almost reached an impasse.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I intend to deal solely with the bill before us, which concerns itself with air pollution control. As I said before, I think the bill is quite inadequate as a piece of legislation. It is nothing more than a vehicle for discussion, and on that basis I give it my approval. It makes no provision whatever for the enforcement of pollution control; in fact, there is nothing new in the bill, because such control as it does provide is already in effect. Nor does it make provision for federal financial involvement, except in a very indirect way. I think there must be
March 1, 1968

financial involvement on the part of the federal government, and for several reasons, one of which is that other jurisdictions have been unable to take action to control pollution, owing to lack of funds.
The bill makes provision for the establishment of a national anti-war pollution agency and a national anti-air pollution advisory council. I do not think we need two bodies where one would do, Mr. Speaker. Second, I do not think that this bill gives the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) any powers additional to those he already has. I am not sure that I like the setting up of another agency for air pollution control only. Neither do I like the setting up of an agency that has no powers of enforcement and no financial resources. The central pivot of the bill is clause 3, which merely sets out the duties of the minister, permitting him to consider certain expediencies but giving him no additional powers.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I would not support the bill as a legislative measure. It has no real strength in the areas I have mentioned, and as a legislative measure is no answer to the serious pollution problems we are now facing. However, as I say, as a vehicle for discussion in this house, and in committee if the bill should be sent there, the bill does have some validity in that it talks about air pollution control. But that is about all it does do. The need for pollution control in this country is so great that, even in its present state, I would not want to oppose the bill. If it does anything at all to meet the situation, then to that extent I support it, just to get some discussion under way.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST GOVERNMENT AND PRIVATE CONTROL AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on Bill C-25, which deals with the control of air pollution. My thoughts are similar to those of the speaker who just preceded me. While the bill is perhaps a good avenue for discussion, it certainly will not go very far in solving pollution problems in this country as we know them today.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that when we talk about air pollution we must also consider other areas of pollution, such as those affecting soil and water. Pollution in the air eventually finds its way to our foliage, then into the soil and into our streams, lakes and rivers, where it tends to become concentrated. Therefore I do not think we can separate these three areas; they must all be considered together. If they are separated, the legislation will suffer by oversimplifying the problem.
Control of Air Pollution
It is my belief that this bill will generate some discussion and to that extent it has some validity. I support it on the ground that it will engender debate across the country by various committees, agencies and groups of people, who would at least be talking about pollution.
I also believe that the problem of pollution has to be tackled on a national scale. Jurisdiction over pollution control is now vested mainly in the provinces, which in turn pass on the responsibility to the various municipalities. The municipalities are reluctant to enforce any legislation that may be detrimental to their economic health. That is to say, they are not anxious to legislate against industry. It is well known that, if they do so, industries move to other areas that allow them to continue to pollute the air their production processes. Therefore it is very rarely that a municipality passes legislation to rigidly control pollution, or even if it does pass legislation, that it enforces that legislation, because the municipality does not want to drive industry out of one community and into a more receptive neighbouring municipality.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, by attacking the problem on a national scale you avoid this sort of competition between municipalities. This concept could also be projected into the provincial field, so that one province does not have more rigid pollution control than its neighbour province, thus inviting industries to jump the provincial border to escape the cost of controlling pollution. I think it is only proper to discuss pollution on a national scale, and I suggest the federal government should assert its authority so that the matter can be attacked nationally. There should be a national law to cover pollution. It ought not to be left to the provinces, since standards of enforcement and legislation are different as between provinces.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Pollution will not be tackled adequately until the general public becomes aware of the menace. There is a growing trend for those working with the press, radio and television to give wide exposure to the dangers of pollution. I recall a program the C.B.C. carried, I believe on February 12, in which the camera and camera crew had been smuggled into the International Nickel plant at Sudbury. Pictures of pollution in the making were taken, pictures which had never been taken before. The president of the company had said that

March 1, 1968
Control of Air Pollution the camera crew would not be allowed in the plant, because it was against company policy, but the photographs had been taken by the time the permission to take them was sought.
Full marks must be given to the C.B.C. This matter might have been discussed during the broadcasting bill discussions. A private station, I think, would never have taken the risk of offending such a large advertiser. It would not have taken such pictures, showing pollution in the making. The C.B.C. crew deserve a medal for bringing this problem to the attention of the public in such a dramatic way.
I also understand that one of the camera crew, after coming out of the smelter, had to receive medical attention on account of the large quantity of sulphur dioxide he had inhaled. In this connection I should put on the record that pollution within the smelter reaches 200 parts of sulphur dioxide per million. That is almost a lethal limit. The medical profession believes that we cannot survive for more than four hours if we breathe a mixture of 200 sulphur dioxide parts per million parts of air. This pollution level exists almost daily in the plant. I must also point out that thousands of men are exposed daily to even higher concentrations of sulphur dioxide, and to ammonia and carbon dioxide.
You can breathe in up to four parts per million of sulphur dioxide without knowing you are breathing pulluted air. Only when the level rises from five to six parts per million does one begin to suffer any discomfort; but it is too late then, because already you have been exposed too much. So, polluted air may be damaging you, and you may not know it. That is the insidious part of pollution, because often you do not know you are exposed to it.

speechtext:
The smell is obnoxious, but whether it is dangerous I do not know. It may be damaging to our sense of smell only.
I have been concerned about the problem of pollution for a number of years. I come from Sudbury, which often takes a drubbing from correspondents who pass through but seldom stay. Invariably you hear statements such as, "It looks like the far side of the moon." One man actually said, "Where did the bomb fall?" There are no forests in our area; they were stripped away many years ago. Without their protection our soil has

eroded and black, barren rocks are exposed. Many wonder why anybody lives there. But we do produce wealth. When that wealth is produced, sulphur dioxide is discharged into the air, and the fumes have ruined one of the most beautiful parts of Canada. One of the best stands of white pine in this country stood in our part of northern Ontario. Now it has been devastated. The topsoil is washed away. Nothing is left except eroded, clay gul-lys and black, barren rocks.
We have a high incidence of lung disease. Though there has been no investigation, I suspect that long term exposure to sulphur dioxide fumes is the cause of it.
Father Hod Marshall of St. Charles College in Sudbury, which is run by the Basilian Fathers, asks in a letter:
Please keep me informed on what progress is being made in that direction. Who was responsible for clearing up a like problem in Trail, B.C.?
The reverend father was referring to our pollution problem. It will be recalled that Trail, in British Columbia, had a problem similar to that of Sudbury. A smelter was refining lead and zinc, and S02 was being exhausted in the process. The provincial government took no action; no government in this country took action. All the same, the fumes were finding their way down into the United States and were damaging the fruit orchards in the state of Washington. The United States government saw fit to bring action against Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, with the result that the company was forced to clean up its operation. The exhaust which polluted the air was turned into fertilizer. So the company turned a waste product into a product that brought it profits.
If a foreign government could bring a punitive action which forced an industry to clean up its manufacturing process, why cannot this government take punitive measures just as effectively to force other industries to clean up their operations.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Some time ago I saw fit to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) the following question about pollution in Sudbury:
Will the Minister of National Health and Welfare undertake a survey to determine the effects on workers of long-term exposure to high concentrations of sulphur dioxide fumes at the International Nickel Company plant in the Sudbury district?
March 1, 1968

To this, the minister replied:
The Department of National Health and Welfare would assist the provincial government, if requested, in conducting a survey of this type.
So you see, Mr. Speaker, there is a problem about determining who has jurisdiction over air pollution control measures. In this instance I was referred to the provincial government. I followed the matter up and referred my question, together with the minister's reply, to Dr. Dymond, minister of health for Ontario, who replied to me as follows:
This will acknowledge receipt of your letter of January 11th. It will also advise you that a study of possible long term effects of exposure to sulphur dioxide in smelter workers and others has already commenced at the Sudbury plant.
I was pleased to hear that this survey had begun. I had been in contact with the local union which was watching this situation closely and I advised the international representative of the United Steel Workers of America, Mr. Valentine, of the information I had been given. He went to the International Nickel Company at whose plant in Sudbury this survey was supposedly taking place, and he afterwards wrote to me in this vein:
I made it a point to contact Mr. Seli, manager of industrial relations for Inco in Sudbury, and asked him if he knew of any studies regarding the possible long term effects of exposure to sulphur dioxide of smelter workers or others in the Sudbury area. To say the least, I was very surprised when he told me he knew nothing about this.
So you see, Mr. Speaker, there is confusion here. The manager of industrial relations in the plant supposedly under study does not even know that the province of Ontario is conducting a survey, if indeed a survey is going forward. The union representative does not know about it, and neither do I, though I am convinced such a survey should be carried out because insufficient information is available as to the effect of sulphur dioxide upon people who are exposed to it; and if ever there was a group of guinea pigs it is this group of five or six thousand workers, some of whom have been exposed for as long as thirty years. A comparison could be made between the condition of their lungs and those of the newer workers, so as to document forever the type of damage which sulphur dioxide does. I think that sulphur dioxide is the main cause of pollution at the present time.
Control of Air Pollution
With regard to this survey in the Sudbury district, on February 2 the Ontario department of mines issued a press release which stated:
The Ontario Department of Health in co-operation with the Ontario Department of Mines has been engaged in a study of the possible health effects of long-term exposure to sulphur dioxide among workers in the Sudbury area. This study is being carried out to determine whether there has been any relationship between work exposure to sulphur dioxide and the occurrence of certain chronic diseases such as respiratory or heart disease.
This is the statement made by the Ontario department of mines and the Ontario department of health. Yet the company does not know about it, the union does not know about it and I do not know about it. It seems strange that a survey could be going on without anyone concerned knowing about it.
There are other people who are concerned about pollution. I have been in contact with Dr. W. Y. Watson, chairman of the biology department at Laurentian University in the city of Sudbury, whose ideas on the subject of pollution are in some respects at variance with my own, and apparently at variance with those of the hon. member who is sponsoring the bill before us. Dr. Watson did attend the conference on pollution held in November, and he writes as follows:
One impression I got from being there was that there was sufficient legislation to begin pollution control.
This professor feels there is sufficient legislation on the books. I shall not quibble with him. I do not believe we have sufficient legislation to enable us to enforce the measures we believe should be taken. If it is the case that there is already sufficient legislation, we do not need Bill C-25, which is a new bill dealing with pollution, though I believe it is a good bill as far as it goes. Dr. Watson goes on to say that the laws and regulations may have to be modified as further research indicates weaknesses.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to make a few comments on Bill No. C-25 introduced by my colleague for Toronto-Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz).
It is now recognized that air pollution is a problem with which our modern world will

March 1, 1963
Control of Air Pollution have to cope and which is liable to upset the economy of all countries.
This pollution is so obvious in urban centres that there is no doubt about it, since buildings are altered, metals are corroded by air acidity or vegetables are dying or are unable to reach maturity. How can men, in turn, avoid the effects of such pollution?
One can say that very few countries do not feel the ill effects of this progressive intoxication caused by air pollution which, contrary to the classic social calamities, affect the countries with the highest standard of living. Therefore, it is in the most developed or industrialized countries, where there is the greatest number of motor vehicles, that the air is increasingly polluted and becomes less and less respirable. When pollution reaches a certain critical stage, unfavorable atmospheric conditions may cause serious diseases and even, in some cases, death.
The Montreal Dimanche Matin, in its last Sunday issue, has denounced the danger of poisonous carbon monoxide emanations in downtown Montreal. Mr. Jean Marier, director of the Air Pollution Division of the Montreal Health Department said in that article that tests have been made in this regard. One of their inspectors spent several days cruising around the downtown section of Montreal as a passenger in a car. The ventilation system of the car was working perfectly and the windows were down. Here are the results of these tests:
The tests have shown a proportion of 12 per cent of carbon monoxide, originating from the exhaust system of various vehicles, in the blood stream of the inspector. This means that 12 per cent of the red corpuscles could not function and absorb the oxygen.
"When there is more than 10 per cent carbon monoxide, there are slight poisoning symptoms, nausea, general discomfort. Between 15 and 20 per cent, there is dizziness and the judgment and faculties become unbalanced. Between 50 and 60 per cent, death strikes rapidly.''
The world has already witnessed similar tragedies and no one can deny that a large city, where such conditions prevail, suffers similar consequences.
In the last few years, we have noticed a considerable decrease in the sunlight and a progressive increase in the fog in industrial areas. The reputation of the notorious "smog" (smoke and fog together), which affects London is universally recognized.
Among the cities which have suffered the most from air pollution, one can single out the city of London, England, where it caused a great number of deaths and disabilities.

During the winter of 1952, everybody remembers that due to a persistent smog which spread all kinds of air impurities, 4,000 persons died and hospitals were filled with the victims of that scourge.
It will also be recalled that as the smog-a combination of smoke and fog-increased, hospitals and other medical centres had to admit only the more severely affected patients. Most of the sick had acute respiratory ailments.
However, humans were not the only ones to be affected, as I said earlier. Some animals, taking part in a show at that time, died or had to be destroyed, due to acute respiratory trouble. All animals were affected, and those who survived required intensive care.
This is the worst disaster of its kind, although London has registered losses from this scourge before and since 1952. The death registers show that already in 1874 there was a number of deaths due to air pollution. The same happened in other parts of the world.
In 1930, in the industrial regions of the Meuse valley, in Belgium, 60 people died and several others were gravely ill during a rather long period of fog which polluted the area. A number of domestic animals died on that occasion.
Closer to home, in Donora, in Pennsylvania, 20 persons died and half the people became ill in similar circumstances in 1948. More recently, New York has started to feel the fatal effects of air pollution.
This proves beyond a doubt that air pollution can cause death or illness which can leave people disabled. The most striking fact in the above examples, is that before people began to suffer from the harmful effects mentioned, pollution seemed to be a normal and harmless phenomenon.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
In London, for instance, the day fog appeared, visibility was good in the morning but at a certain time, when the velocity of the wind came to nearly nothing, pollution started to cover the city. The next day, smog became so dense that some transportation companies had to stop all activities. Traffic practically stopped and many drivers left their cars in the streets. So the city of London became virtually crippled during four days because of fog.
What will happen if similar conditions occur again? One can wonder to what extent people living in a city where air is polluted
March 1, 1968



are affected in a normal day. There is always in the air this mixture of smoke, sulphur dioxide and possibly other noxious substances, but those substances do not present as much danger as when the atmosphere is calm.
Medical authorities are not unanimous on this point, but it is getting more obvious that some illnesses, like bronchitis, emphysema and other respiratory ailments are aggravated, if not caused, by daily exposure to an atmosphere considered as normal, but containing a certain degree of pollution. It is also suspected that lung cancer is caused by air pollution, but to a lower degree than by cigaret smoke.
It has been proved that people living in cities where the pollution danger is more pronounced are more subject to lung cancer than those who live in rural areas. It is not necessary to have been subjected to air pollution all our life to pay the consequences, because it has been clearly demonstrated that people who have emigrated from the United Kingdom to Australia or South Africa are more subject to lung cancer than those who were born and had always lived in those countries.
In addition to the human deaths which result from air pollution, there is also a considerable loss of human resources. Vegetation is hampered, livestock suffer from almost incurable diseases, houses and buildings are blackened and man is even deprived of the pleasure of admiring the beauties of nature. Estimates have been made of the losses incurred, and it is generally accepted that air pollution costs urban dwellers between $30 and $40 a year per capita.
In Canada, it means that air pollution can cost billions of dollars annually. We could subsidize several programs, in order to control that problem with a small percentage of those funds. All citizens should contribute to those expenditures incurred for the control of pollution which is permeating our towns and cities.
Sources of pollution are various and I will simply summarize them. We have just completed some investigations and the knowledge gained on the subject throughout the country should be efficiently conveyed. We know that Bill No. C-25 includes provisions to that effect. The bill asks the minister to recognize the urgent necessity of encouraging research at the municipal, provincial and federal levels, in order to determine the nature of air pollution and the means to control it.
The bill is also concerned with research on atmospheric conditions and air quality in
Public Accounts
order to establish criteria and national standards. Special appropriations are also contained in this bill in order to promote research at the university level and to facilitate the exchange of knowledge between various intermediary bodies which the department intends to establish.
Mr. Speaker, those points are among the most important and they are conformable to my earlier remarks. We must be informed on that matter. We cannot be satisfied to pass legislation in the hope that the problem will be solved in that way. We must also be sure that the course of action which we shall follow will meet adequately and in all respects, the interest of the country.
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh):
That the bill be referred to the standing committee on health and welfare.
